reason: The molecule has an aziridine N and a CH2OH side chain. The three-membered ring is rigid, so conformer energies are dominated by intramolecular O-H···N hydrogen bonding, torsional staggering around the C-C bonds, and close nonbonded contacts. I first measured the O···N and H···N distances and estimated whether the O-H vector points toward the N lone pair. Conformers with short H···N distances (roughly 2.15-2.35 Å) and reasonable O-H···N direction were placed highest. Within that group, I penalized conformers with near-eclipsed heavy-atom torsions: e.g. 10 and 29 have excellent H-bond geometry but both C2-C3-C6-N and C3-C6-C14-O are nearly eclipsed; 7, 15 and 30 have one near-eclipsed chain torsion; 5 has a very short H-bond but a slightly close methyl···oxygen contact. Conformers without an O-H···N H-bond were placed lower, especially those that fold the OH near N without achieving H-bonding, which leaves lone-pair/steric repulsion without compensation. Extended non-hydrogen-bonded conformers are intermediate. The final ordering is approximate within closely spaced clusters, but the clearest separation is between the H-bonded set, the extended non-H-bonded set, and the folded non-H-bonded set.

The molecule contains an amide (NH2), an amine (NH), a carbonyl (C=O), and a nitrile (C≡N). The dominant intramolecular stabilizers are H-bonds: amide N-H to the amine N (N-H···N), amine N-H to the carbonyl O (N-H···O=C), and weaker amide N-H to the nitrile N. I estimated H···acceptor distances and N-H···A angles from the coordinates. The most stable conformers have very short, well-directed H-bonds: 30, 27, 19, and 7 all have amide N-H···N distances near 2.11 Å with angles ~109-110°, giving the strongest intramolecular H-bonding. Next come 18, 15, 25, and 13, also with strong amide N-H···N H-bonds but slightly longer H···N distances (2.15-2.18 Å). Conformers 22, 29, and 20 have strong amine N-H···O=C H-bonds with H···O 2.19-2.22 Å and angles ~108-111°, somewhat less stabilizing than the best amide-amine H-bonds. Moderate H-bonds follow: 28, 1, 5, 24, 4, and 10. Conformers 21 and 17 have two weak H-bonds (N-H···O and N-H···N≡C), while 6, 11, and 14 have weaker or poorly-directed contacts. 9 and 23 have only weak nitrile H-bonds. The least stable are conformers with no well-directed H-bond and some close nonbonded contacts (16, 2, 26, 8), and finally 12 and 3 lack any significant intramolecular H-bond. Ordering within similar H-bond types is uncertain, but the overall trend is based on H-bond strength and donor-acceptor directionality.

All conformers are ethyl 2-aminopropanoate. The dominant stabilizing feature is intramolecular N-H...O=C hydrogen bonding (5-membered ring, N-H...O angle ~104°) when the amine H points toward the carbonyl oxygen; this is seen in conformers 2, 5, 6, 20, 21, 23 (H...O ~2.35 Å, N...O ~2.78 Å). A weaker N-H...O(ester) H-bond to the ether oxygen is present in 7, 12, 18, 22, 25 (H...O ~2.35-2.52 Å, angle ~99-106°) and is less stabilizing because the ether O is a poorer acceptor. Folded conformers without a donor-aligned H-bond (1, 3, 17, 26, 29, 30) place N and O=C in close 1,4-gauche contact without the compensating H-bond; they are less stable. Remaining extended conformers have no H-bond and close N...O(ether) contacts, making them least stable. Steric H...H contacts are all greater than ~2.35 Å, so no severe repulsion dominates; within each group the ordering is based on small H-bond distance/angle differences and avoiding even minor close contacts. Uncertainty remains within the groups, especially among the non-H-bonded conformers.

The molecule is an acyclic propargyl ether alcohol (CH3-C≡C-CH2-O-CH2-CH(OH)-CH3). The dominant conformation-dependent stabilizing interaction is intramolecular O-H···ether-O hydrogen bonding between the hydroxyl donor (O8-H9) and the ether oxygen O5. I evaluated O5···H9 distances, O5···O8 distances, and approximate O-H···O direction; conformers with O5···H9 near 2.2-2.35 Å and O5···O8 near 2.77-2.80 Å are treated as H-bonded and therefore more stable. Among these, extra destabilizing contacts were assessed by looking at the C4-O5-C6-C7 and O5-C6-C7-C10 gauche arrangements: conformers with both the propargyl arm and the C7 methyl placed anti to the ether oxygen (e.g. 19, 28, 3, 18) avoid additional gauche strain, while 2, 13, 24, 7 have very short H-bonds but carry one additional O-C-C-C/O-C-C-O gauche interaction. Conformers 11, 14, 16, 27 still have H-bonds but have a close O5···C10 gauche contact, making them somewhat less stable. Non-H-bonded conformers are ranked next; those with anti O-C-C-O and anti C4-C7 arrangements (22, 29, 9, 10) are the most stable of this group, followed by anti O-C-C-O but gauche C4-C7 contacts (23, 12, 4, 6, 1). The remaining conformers lack H-bonds and have gauche or skew O-C-C-O arrangements with additional close contacts; 30, 25, 17 are gauche O-C-C-O without H-bonding, while 5, 8, 21, 20, 15 have skew/eclipsed-like O-C-C-O torsions and are considered less stable. Several near-degenerate rotamers are difficult to separate with certainty, especially within the H-bonded cluster, but the ranking below reflects the best geometric compromise between H-bond strength and torsional/steric strain.

All conformers share the same cyclopropane-diol connectivity. The main stability differences come from intramolecular O-H...O hydrogen bonding between the two hydroxyl groups, followed by steric contacts between the isopropyl methyl groups and the hydroxyl oxygens / cyclopropane ring. Using the coordinates, the best H-bond is in Conformer 6: short O...O distance (~2.66 Å), short H...O distance (~2.04 Å), and a favorable O-H...O angle (~120°). Conformers 14, 25, 17, 21, 5, 18, 3, 30, 26, 11, 27, and 2 also show progressively weaker or more distorted O-H...O approaches. Conformer 4, 20, and 9 have short O...O contacts but poor H-bond geometry, so their close O...O approach is mainly repulsive/unfavorable. Many remaining non-H-bonded conformers have similar energies; they were ranked by the severity of close methyl-to-oxygen contacts and by avoiding simultaneous bad eclipsing interactions. The middle/lower part of the ranking is uncertain because differences are subtle and no thermodynamic data are provided.

The molecule is an N-(1-methoxybutan-2-yl)aziridine. All conformers keep the same aziridine ring connectivity and essentially the same ring invertomer, so the ranking is governed by side-chain torsional strain and steric/lone-pair contacts. The most important torsion is N-C(alpha)-C(ethyl)-CH3: anti avoids a close N...CH3 gauche contact. Next, N-C(alpha)-CH2-O anti avoids N...O lone-pair repulsion. Finally, C(alpha)-CH2-O-CH3 prefers anti over gauche, and values near 100-115 are close to O-C-C/H eclipsing maxima and are disfavored. Conformer 2 is uniquely all-anti across the three key side-chain torsions, making it the most stable. Conformers 10, 20, 24, and 30 have N/ethyl anti and N/O anti but OMe gauche; they form the next tier. Conformer 3 has the OMe anti but N/O gauche; it sits just below that tier. The E-anti conformers with additional O/OMe strain are next, followed by E-gauche conformers with otherwise good O/OMe arrangements. The least stable conformers are those with near-eclipsed O-CH3 or O-C-C torsion values: 29 has an OMe torsion near 114, and 18 has an N-C-C-O torsion near 130 with an ethyl-gauche interaction. The ordering within similar groups is based on small deviations from ideal staggered angles and close N...CH3 contacts.

The molecule is a seven-carbon diol with two OH groups: a secondary OH on the central branch point and a primary OH at the chain terminus. I examined the coordinates for intramolecular O-H...O hydrogen bonds by computing O...O distances, H...O distances, and approximate O-H...O angles, and I also checked for close nonbonded C...C and C...O contacts. Conformers with short, linear H-bonds (O...O near 2.7-2.8 Å, H...O near 1.8 Å, angle >150°) are ranked highest, especially 21, 26, 22, and 29. Conformers such as 28, 24, 16, 14, 30, 17, and 15 also have strong H-bonds but have slightly longer H...O distances, poorer angles, or additional gauche O-C-C-C contacts. Among H-bonded conformers, 7 is penalized by a close 1,5 methyl-methyl contact (~3.35 Å), while 1 and 3 have longer, less linear H-bonds and are lower in the H-bonded group. Conformers 5, 6, 9, and 12 have O...O close enough for possible weak H-bonding but the O-H...O angles are poor, so they fall in the middle. Conformers 4, 11, 13, 18, 20, 23, 25, and 27 lack a usable intramolecular H-bond; among these, 11 and 13 are relatively extended with less obvious crowding, whereas 20 has a close methyl-methyl contact (~3.40 Å) and 23/25 have close O...C contacts (~3.10 Å), making them least stable. The later part of the ranking is uncertain because several differences are subtle.

All 30 structures share the same cyclopropane-containing skeleton with a methyl ketone side chain and two hydroxyl groups (one on the cyclopropane carbon bearing the side chain, one on the adjacent cyclopropane carbon). Since the cyclopropane ring strain is essentially constant, the main stability differences come from intramolecular hydrogen bonding to the ketone carbonyl and from steric crowding. I evaluated O-H...O=C distances and H-bond directionality from the coordinates. The most stabilized conformers are those with a strong O10-H...O3 H-bond (H...O around 1.9-2.0 Å and near-linear O-H...O angle): 4, 18, 9, 8, and 20; 3 is also strong but slightly less linear. Conformer 26, 22, 19, 23, and 29 have good O15-H...O3 H-bonds; 13 has a bifurcated but less directional pair of weak H-bonds and is placed after the good single H-bonds. Conformers 12, 27, and 30 have moderate O10-H...O3 H-bonds, while 28, 1, 5, and 10 are weaker or poorly aligned. The remaining conformers lack a strong intramolecular H-bond and are ranked mainly by steric clashes: 24, 11, 14, 6, and 25 are relatively open or only mildly crowded, whereas 7, 15, 2, 21, 17, and 16 have increasingly unfavorable methyl-cyclopropane or methyl-hydroxyl contacts. Conformer 16 has the shortest C1-C7 contact and multiple close O/C nonbonded contacts, making it the least stable. The middle/lower rankings are subtle and some adjacent choices are uncertain.

The molecule is CH3-CH(OH)-CH(CHO)-COCH3 (a secondary alcohol with an aldehyde and a methyl ketone on the adjacent carbon). The dominant stabilizing factor is an intramolecular O-H...O=C hydrogen bond from the hydroxyl group to one of the two carbonyl oxygens. I identified 12 conformers with genuine O-H...O H-bonds (H...O roughly 1.9-2.25 Å, O-H...O roughly 123-138 degrees): 17, 15, 4, 10, 18, 23, 29, 24, 22, 5, 14, 21. Conformer 17 has the strongest H-bond (H...O 1.92 Å, angle 138 degrees, ketone acceptor) and also a favorable antiparallel carbonyl dipole arrangement, so it is the most stable. Conformers 15, 4, and 10 are the next tier: 15 has an excellent aldehyde-accepted H-bond (2.01 Å, 133 degrees) and the two C=O dipoles are almost perfectly antiparallel; 4 has a ketone-accepted H-bond of similar distance but a slightly worse angle; 10 is close behind with a slightly longer ketone H-bond. The remaining H-bonded conformers are ranked by decreasing H-bond quality and increasing steric contacts, so 18 and 23 are next, then 29, 24, and 22, and finally 5, 14, and 21 which have the longest/most bent H-bonds. Conformer 13 has only a very weak and bent O-H...O contact (3.02 Å, 107 degrees) and is treated as effectively non-H-bonded. Among the non-H-bonded conformers, 12 and 19 show short n-to-pi* carbonyl contacts (ketone O approaching the aldehyde carbonyl C at 2.75 and 2.88 Å with Bürgi-Dunitz-like angles of 111-114 degrees), making them the most stable of this set. Conformers 7, 1, 27, and 6 have moderate C-H...O contacts (H...O 2.21-2.25 Å, angles 122-127 degrees) and appear next. A second tier of weak C-H...O interactions places 11, 26, 9, 28, 25, and 8 above the conformers with no specific stabilizing contact. The least stable conformers (16, 30, 3, 2, 20) lack both O-H...O and significant weak contacts; 20 has a parallel/repulsive C=O dipole orientation and is placed last. The middle of the ranking, especially among 5/14/21 and 1/6/7/27/13, is uncertain because the energy differences are only a few kJ/mol, but the ordering of the strongly H-bonded top group is robust.

The main stabilizing feature is an intramolecular O-H...π contact with the C5=C6 double bond: favorable when the hydroxyl hydrogen lies near both C6 and C5 (H-O to C6 ≈ 2.49–2.53 Å, H-O to C5 ≈ 2.7–2.8 Å). Conformers with this geometry and the methyl group anti to the ring nitrogen are placed highest. The methyl-anti arrangement avoids a mild H···H contact with N-H; methyl-syn conformers are still reasonable but slightly penalized. No true linear N-H...O or O-H...N hydrogen bond exists because the donor-H···acceptor angles are poor; many supposedly close O···N contacts have the H atom pointing away. The clearly worst structures are 12 and 20, where the OH proton points away from the C=C π system and the O atom is forced very close to N (≈2.70 Å) with H···O ≈ 2.41 Å but a poor hydrogen-bond geometry, and 25, which has a severe methyl/N-H steric clash. Structures with only C6-directed O-H but no C5 component are intermediate. The ordering within the middle is uncertain because the energy differences are subtle and depend on small compromises between π-H-bond geometry, methyl orientation, and weak nonbonded contacts.

The molecule is a flexible quaternary alcohol bearing methyl, CH2CHO, and CH2C≡CH substituents. The dominant stabilizing interaction is intramolecular O–H···O=C hydrogen bonding. From the coordinates, six conformers have a genuine O–H···O=C contact with H···O distances below about 2.15 Å and O–H···O angles near 124–141°: 1, 16, 2, 6, 21, and 26. Among these, 1 is clearly best (H···O ≈ 1.94 Å, angle ≈ 141°), followed by 16 and 2, then 6, 21, and 26. For the remaining conformers, the OH is not well oriented toward the aldehyde carbonyl. Several instead show weaker O–H···π(alkyne) contacts: 22, 28, 7, 19, 23, 30, 13, 4, 12, 11, 9, 8, and 17, ordered approximately by H-to-alkyne midpoint distance and directionality. Conformer 25 has a weak C–H···O=C interaction but no good O–H···π contact, so it is placed after the O–H···π group. The remaining structures are more extended or have only ordinary steric contacts; among them, 5, 15, 29, 14, 10, 24, 20, 18, and 27 are ranked before 3 because 3 has a close O···O contact without a proper hydrogen-bond geometry, which is slightly destabilizing. The lower-middle part of the ranking is uncertain because steric and weak dispersion differences are subtle.

The molecule is a substituted tetrahydrofuran (C7H14O2) with one ring ether oxygen and one terminal hydroxyl oxygen. The dominant stabilizing intramolecular interaction is an O-H...O hydrogen bond from the side-chain hydroxyl to the ring ether oxygen. Strong hydrogen-bonded conformers show O-H...O distances around 1.98-2.10 Å, O...O distances around 2.77-2.81 Å, and reasonable O-H...O angles; these are placed at the top. Conformer 13 has a longer, weaker O-H...O contact and is ranked after the well-formed H-bonded set. Among the non-hydrogen-bonded conformers, those with extended anti side-chain conformations and no close O/O or methyl/hydroxyl contacts are ranked higher; gauche but still non-clashing side chains are intermediate; folded conformers that bring the hydroxyl oxygen near the ring ether oxygen without forming an H-bond are ranked lower because of unfavorable O-O contacts and steric strain. The middle and lower ranks are uncertain because the energetic differences are subtle and estimated mainly from geometry.

The molecule is an open-chain imino ether aldehyde (C5H9NO2) with no rings. I analyzed the coordinates for intramolecular N-H...O H-bonds: the only donor is N-H (H15) and acceptors are aldehyde O7 and ether O12. In all conformers H15...O12 is nearly fixed ~3.15 Å and H15...O7 is >2.8 Å with poor N-H...O angles (~110-130°), so no strong H-bond forms. The main stability differences come from staggered vs eclipsed/gauche arrangements along the two central C-C bonds. The most important preferences are: (i) the aldehyde oxygen O7 anti to the bulky CH2-O-imine side chain (C9-O7 distance ~3.4-3.6 Å) rather than gauche (~2.8 Å); and (ii) the ether oxygen O12 anti to the aldehyde group (C6-O12 distance >3.6 Å) rather than gauche (~2.9 Å). Only conformers 11, 2, and 27 satisfy both anti relationships; among them 11 is most regular, 2 has a short C-H...O contact, and 27 has a closer methyl-imine contact. Conformers 25,19,12,13 retain O12-anti but have O7 gauche to the side chain, so they are next. Then come extended conformers that keep O7 anti but place O12 gauche to the aldehyde; within this group, longer C1...N14 distances and absence of close N...O contacts raise stability (e.g. 8,16,20,7,10,29,26,28,18,5,6). Folded conformers with short N...O7 contacts (2.6-2.7 Å) but no linear H-bond, and/or C1...N14 contacts near 3.2-3.5 Å, are penalized and occupy the lower part; the least stable are the most compact/eclipsed structures 24,15,4,3, with 3 showing the most severe combination of close contacts and gauche interactions. The ordering is semi-quantitative because eclipsing penalties and weak C-H...O contacts are subtle.

The molecule is a substituted cyclohexene: a six-membered ring with one C=C (C-D bond ~1.32 Å), a methyl on the allylic carbon B, and a CH2OH group at carbon F. Using the plane through the three alkene/adjacent atoms C-D-E, I classified ring puckering by whether F and G lie on opposite sides (half-chair, lower strain) or the same side (boat/twist, higher strain). I also assigned the methyl and hydroxymethyl groups as cis/trans by whether their key carbons lie on the same or opposite sides of this plane. The most important stabilizing interaction is an intramolecular OH...pi hydrogen bond when the hydroxyl hydrogen sits close to the C=C double bond. This is strongest for conformers 20, 10, 16, 26, 7, and 23 (OH...C=C distances about 2.3-2.7 Å). Among these, 20 and 10 combine the H-bond with a half-chair-like ring, so they are ranked highest. The half-chair trans conformers without H-bonding (2, 12, 3, 24, 11, 8, 21, 28, 25) are next because they avoid 1,3-diaxial-type strain and have no severe nonbonded contacts. Then come half-chair cis conformers that lack the compensating OH...pi contact (18, 1, 4, 14, 9, 13); their same-face methyl/CH2OH arrangement creates minor steric crowding. The boat-like conformers with OH...pi H-bonding (16, 26, 7, 23) follow, since the H-bond only partially offsets boat strain. The remaining boat conformers without H-bonding are increasingly strained, with the worst having close methyl/CH2OH contacts and poor ring puckering. The ordering is approximate in the middle groups, where the energies differ only subtly, but the extremes are robust.

All 30 structures share the same connectivity: a formamide N-H/C=O end, a flexible alkyl chain, a branched CH, a methyl group, and a terminal CH2OH. The dominant intramolecular stabilizing feature is therefore a donor-acceptor hydrogen bond. The strongest class is O-H···O=C, where the terminal hydroxyl hydrogen approaches the formyl carbonyl oxygen: conformers 20, 29, 3, 4, 24, 7, 17, 28, 8, and 11 have short O-H···O=C contacts in the 1.87–2.10 Å range with roughly linear O-H···O angles. These should be most stable. Within this group I ranked by H-bond distance/linearity and by avoiding close H···H contacts; e.g. 20 has the shortest O-H···O=C contact and fewer steric clashes, while 8 and 11 have longer/less ideal H-bonds. The next class is N-H···O-H hydrogen bonding, where the amide N-H donates to the hydroxyl oxygen: conformers 5, 9, 14, 27, and 16 show N-H···O distances near 1.9–2.0 Å. They are still stabilized, but this donor-acceptor pair is generally weaker than the O-H···C=O hydrogen bond. Conformers 19, 25, 18, 23, and 6 have weaker or more distorted N-H···O-H interactions and are placed lower. The remaining conformers lack a strong intramolecular hydrogen bond and are ranked lower; among these, the ordering is more uncertain and reflects mainly the absence of obvious severe clashes and relatively benign folded/extended geometries.

All 30 conformers share the same connectivity: a primary alcohol, a secondary alcohol, and an aziridine N–H are the main polar groups. The dominant stability factor is intramolecular hydrogen bonding: O–H···N is strongest, O–H···O is next, and N–H···O is weaker. Conformer 2 is uniquely well set up with both O1–H···N and O2–H···O1 H-bonds, so it is the most stable. Conformer 23 has a very short, nearly linear O1–H···N H-bond and is second. Next come conformers with one good O–H···O H-bond; among these, 12 also has a moderately directional N–H···O contact, so it leads that group. Conformers 3, 21, 29, 14, and 16 have short/linear O–H···O bonds and are placed next, with small differences in distance/linearity and weak auxiliary interactions separating them. The remaining O–H···O-containing conformers follow, ranked by H-bond distance/angle and any weak N–H···O contacts. The least stable group has no strong internal H-bond: 30 has a weak O–H···O contact, 27 a weak O–H···N, 7 a weak N–H···O, and 8 only a very long O–H···N contact; 1, 10, 15, 18, 20, and 26 lack strong H-bonds and are placed at the bottom. There is genuine uncertainty in the middle and lower ordering where distances/angles are very close, and the final permutation should be read with that caveat.

The molecule is a flexible imidate ester with an N-H and a terminal O-H. The dominant stabilising feature is an intramolecular O-H···O(imidate) hydrogen bond, which requires the terminal hydroxymethylene chain to fold back to O5. I checked O···O and H···O distances and donor angles. Strong O-H···O5 H-bonds occur in 5, 9, 13, 8, 17 and 2; among these 5, 9 and 13 have the shortest H···O (~1.87–1.91 Å) and most linear O-H···O angles, 8 is slightly weaker, and 17/2 have longer H···O and poorer angles. Conformer 18 has N-H···O and O-H···N contacts but with poor angles and a very close H···H contact (2.14 Å), so it is less stable than the good O-H···O5 set. Conformer 15 has only a weak, long N-H···O10 contact. The remaining conformers lack a strong intramolecular H-bond. Among those, more extended structures are placed before folded non-hydrogen-bonded structures because the latter pay gauche/strain penalties without gaining H-bond stabilisation; the lowest-energy no-H-bond conformers are the folded ones with O10 near O5/N but with O-H not pointing at an acceptor. The middle section is uncertain because the differences are small.

The molecule is N≡C-CH2-O-CH2-CH2-cyclopropane. No conventional hydrogen-bond donors exist, so ranking is controlled by torsional strain, 1,4-gauche contacts, and skew/eclipsed-type interactions around the three main rotatable bonds: C2-C3-O-C5, C3-O-C5-C6, and O-C5-C6-C7, plus the orientation of the cyclopropyl group. Using heavy-atom 1,4 distances as proxies, conformers with C3...C6 ≈ 3.7 Å and O4...C7 ≈ 3.7 Å are anti around the central C-O-C-C and O-C-C-C units; values near 3.0 Å indicate gauche contacts. All-anti conformers 16 and 30 are the most extended and avoid both O-cyclopropyl and CH2-CH2 gauche strain. 13 and 6 have only a small gauche interaction at the nitrile-bearing CH2-O end, so they follow. 23, 5, and 28 keep the bulky cyclopropyl group anti to oxygen but have a gauche C3...C6 contact; 17 has anti C3...C6 but a gauche O-cyclopropyl contact. Two-gauche and skew conformers (C2...C5 near 3.1 Å, C3...C6 near 3.1-3.3 Å, or O4...C7 near 3.2-3.4 Å) are progressively more strained. There are no severe close H-H clashes in any structure, and many near-degenerate pairs/triplets exist, so the exact order within those groups is uncertain. The overall ranking reflects a decreasing preference for anti over gauche and for pure staggered angles over skew/eclipsed-like torsions.

The molecule is a seven-membered oxepene ring with an exocyclic CH2OH at the alkene carbon and a ring ether oxygen. The largest single stabilizing feature is an intramolecular O-H···O hydrogen bond from the hydroxymethyl OH to the ring ether oxygen. Only conformers 20 and 12 show a credible O-H···Oether contact: O···O ≈ 3.60/3.56 Å, H···O ≈ 2.92/2.89 Å, and O-H···O angles ≈ 131°/127°. These two are therefore the most stable; 20 is slightly more linear, while 12 is slightly shorter, so they are placed at the top, with 20 marginally ahead. Conformers 18 and 8 have O···Oether ≈ 3.6 Å but the H···O distances are >3.2 Å and the O-H···O angles are only about 100°, so these are not real hydrogen bonds; they are ranked next because the CH2OH is still oriented away from severe allylic strain and no close H···H contact is evident. The remaining non-hydrogen-bonded conformers are ordered according to avoidance of 1,3-allylic strain between the hydroxymethyl group and the alkene, the length of the O1-C5 contact, and close H···H contacts. Several conformers have especially short O1-C5 distances and H2-H19 contacts below 2.4 Å, indicating real A1,3 strain: especially 21 (H2-H19 ≈ 2.15 Å), 9, 11, 17, and 10/15 also show close contacts. Conformers 30 and 28 have very short O1-C5 contacts near 2.73 Å, a close O···C vdW clash with the alkene carbon, placing them near the bottom. Conformer 1 is clearly the least stable/unphysical because several of its H positions are inconsistent with the carbon skeleton (the listed H18-H21 are far from any carbon, implying unsatisfied valence), so it is ranked last. The middle ordering among conformers with no strong H-bond and no severe clash is more uncertain; differences there are subtle and mostly governed by small variations in ring pucker and CH2OH placement.

Step-by-step: The only strong intramolecular interaction available is the hydroxyl O-H donor with the ether oxygen. Using the explicit hydroxyl hydrogen coordinates, only conformers 9 and 16 have H···O(ether) distances short enough for a hydrogen bond: 9 has H···O ≈ 2.00 Å, O···O ≈ 2.94 Å and an almost linear O-H···O angle; 16 has H···O ≈ 2.05 Å, O···O ≈ 2.95 Å and is slightly less linear. These two are therefore clearly the most stable, with 9 slightly better than 16. All other conformers have H···O(ether) distances above about 4 Å and lack a hydrogen bond. For the remaining conformers, the ranking is more uncertain; I ordered them by estimated side-chain strain and steric contacts. Conformers with an anti O-C-C-C side-chain arrangement (larger O···C3 distance, extended orientation away from the bicyclic core) are placed higher than gauche or folded conformers. Among gauche/folded non-hydrogen-bonded conformers, those with close O···O contacts or more crowded folded geometries are placed lower, since they have unfavorable 1,4-type O/O and H/H interactions without the compensating hydrogen bond.

The molecule is a cyclobutane bearing a 2-hydroxyethyl side chain and a ring hydroxyl group. The dominant stability factor is intramolecular O-H...O hydrogen bonding. Conformers 30, 1, 9, and 25 have O···O distances near 2.87–2.92 Å and H···O contacts around 1.9–2.0 Å with near-linear donor orientations, so they are ranked highest. Among these, 30 and 25 have better staggered side-chain torsions, while 1 and 9 have more eclipsed C–C side-chain dihedrals and flatter cyclobutane rings; 30 has slightly better H-bond geometry than 25, and 1 is marginally preferred over 9 due to a more linear H-bond, though the 1/9 ordering is subtle. Conformer 18 lacks an H-bond but is uniquely anti-anti in both side-chain C–C bonds with a well-puckered cyclobutane ring, making it the best non-hydrogen-bonded conformer. The next group favors one gauche interaction rather than two: conformers 29, 8, 2, 24, and 7 place the oxygen gauche but the terminal carbon anti, often with weak C–H···O contacts; 7 has a short O–H···H–C contact and is the worst of this group. Conformers 10, 15, 23, 16, 26, and 13 have the O–C bond anti but the internal C–C bond gauche, placing CH2 near the ring; 13 has a slightly more compressed C1···C4 distance.
